1992 must surely have been an pivotal year for Megadeth. Fueled by a solid lineup which would prove to be their longest lasting thus far, they were also fresh off the success of their masterpeice, RUST IN PEACE. A true classic of metal, RUST IN PEACE was the album which finally put Megadeth in a position to potentially challenge Metallica for the heavy metal crown.

Thus it was that, in 1992, they released COUNTDOWN TO EXTINCTION. With its stripped down sounds, the album seemed to be a response to Metallica's massivly successful 'Black Album,' a year earlier. From the first moments of "Skin O' My Teeth," COUNTDOWN reminds us that few can write a guitar riff like Dave Mustaine. "Skiin O' My Teeth" is a great song that starts the album off well, and is immediatly followed us by another stellar bit of Mustaine riffage "Symphony of Distruction." The album continues to display a number a great songs, including "Foreclosure of a Dream" which features a nicely contrasting mellow verse and speedy chorus (plus a none too flattering cameo from then-president George H. W. Bush).

Despite the fact that there are some undeniably excellent songs on this album, it's difficult to avoid noticing that there are some songs on this album which can only be called filler. Sure, "Psychotron" and "Captive Honor" are enjoyable enough to listen to, but they certainly leave no lasting memories once done. The album is also plagued by a bit too much reliance on traditional verse-chorus patterns, making it too predictable in places, which is slightly dissappointing after the twisting progressive epics of RUST IN PEACE.

Overall, it isn't 100% successful, but that doesn't prevent it from being one of the great rock records of the 90s, well deserving of its number two spot on the charts (that it was robbed of number one by "Achey Breaky Heart," of all things, is truly one of the crimes of the century). COUNTDOWN TO EXTINCTION is a great album, well woprthwhile for any fan of rock or metal.

Jimmy Cobb needs no introduction. He is a survivor, who is still alive today. A living legend, he contributes beautiful rhythm and music to this trio.
The songs here are a mix of jazz classics such as Duke Ellington's "Solitude" and Benny Golson's "5 Spot After Dark" and pop oriented hits such as Johnny Mathis' "Wonderful, Wonderful" given a jazz interpretation. They are fun to listen to.

reviews:
Was very disappointed in this release at first. Nary a swaggering distorted blooze guitar riff to be found here. The opener "The Devil" has Polly plunking on the piano and singing very high in an unusual way, which at first put me off though I was fascinated. The songs that follow, "Dear Darkness" and "Grow Grow Grow", may or may not grab you initially, but I guarantee the more you listen they will worm their way into your subconscious. "When Under Ether", the single with its mellow piano lines, is classic Polly, and also encapsultates this entire album: sparse, simple, cryptic and intimate.

I love the title track, with it's banjo and harmonica accompaniment. "Silence", with its busy beat and hurried structure that complements the lyrics, and the completely creepy "To Talk To You", are both incredibly moving songs. "The Piano", which perversely contains little or no actual piano, brings back the nihilistic Polly of olde, with the lines "hit her with a hammer/teeth smashed in". The closer, "The Mountain", with it's cascading piano trills, closes the album with Polly wailing on the mountain, as if straining to be heard over the wind as the track gets noisier. It's an awesome song, and a great closer to one of PJ's landmark albums. With the songs heightened drama, it often reminds me of Thom Yorke's "The Eraser", sans of course any and all electronic embellishment.

Many other artists that I respect as much as Polly have seemingly fallen away in quality of output. But somehow PJ keeps going from strength to strength. It can't be easy to be this challenging yet so listenable, so I can't overstate this enough: she is the standard that every other "important" modern act should be measured against.
title: White Chalk
description: Product Description, White Chalk is PJ HARVEY's eighth studio album and first new material since 2004's critically acclaimed Uh Huh Her. PJ Harvey went into the studio late last year to record and produce with Flood and John Parish. The three had worked together previously on the GRAMMY nominated To Bring You My Love and on Is This Desire?. White Chalk also includes musical contributions from Harvey's long time associate Eric Drew Feldman, and Jim White from The Dirty Three., The album highlights PJ Harvey's incredible ability to consistently create a unique, yet always impactful experience with each new album. Her talents as a songwriter, musician, and producer have never been as powerful, or profound, as on White Chalk. The songs are wonderfully mesmerizing, leaving a hypnotic effect on the listener., Amazon.com, This carnival ride to the netherworld of the soul is PJ Harvey's most dizzyingly radical work since the raw pulse and grind of her 1993 debut. It's also entirely different. Harvey's created an emotionally fractured Gothic fairytale that rides on her spare, tattered piano playing and her voice, which she turns into a fragile siren's call: high, airy, and imperiled, and made otherworldly by a labyrinth of echo. Instead of pop tunes, Harvey offers an 11-song cycle that's the metaphorical story of a breakup in which the Devil, a drug-induced nightmare, and a seemingly bottomless pit of despair all play a part. At the end, in "The Mountain," her banshee wails conclude a journey so oblique it's worthy of David Lynch or Neil Gaiman. Flood, who co-produced Harvey's 1998 epic rock breakthrough, Is This Desire?, with her, reprises that role, but, White Chalk, is more chamber music--and a dark chamber at that., --Ted Drozdowski

reviews:
To begin, it's a shame that it appears that this wonderful soundtrack has been withdrawn from active circulation; it's a perfect companion to the DVD of the film. When "Meet Me in St. Louis" was initially released in 1944, it was before original soundtracks for films were recorded. Judy Garland did record her songs for the Decca label with great success, yet they didn't quite equal the luster and verve of the soundtrack performances. As the fiftieth anniversary of the film approached in 1994, Turner Classic Movies which owned the rights to the movie decided to release for the first time the complete film soundtrack in true Stereophonic Sound under their "Rhino" movie music label. The actual release was off by one year, 1995, but with such magnificent results as were achieved it's hard to quibble over a missed anniversary!

The heart and soul of the film's score are the three original songs that were composed by the young songwriting team of Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane. Even though it's probably redundant to name them if you've seen the film, they are "The Boy Next Door", "The Trolley Song" and "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas". All were masterfully sung by Judy Garland at the absolute peak of her talent, and her renditions made them standards. "The Boy Next Door" has a wistful, yearning quality, a young girl's longing for a young man who has yet not noticed her, it's totally beguiling.

The mega hit was "The Trolley Song" which was a best seller even before the film was released. It also was nominated for an Oscar for Best Song of 1944, but was unfortunately surpassed by "Swingin' on a Star!" from "Going My Way". Judy Garland captured it in one take in the prerecording. According to composer Hugh Martin who was there at the session, although he was thrilled by Ms. Garland's initial rendition she made a very tiny error with the lyrics. He pointed this out to Roger Edens, Garland's superb vocal coach and musical arranger who was largely responsible for her unique vocal style. Edens wisely replied, "Hugh, forget it, the spirit was so marvelous, don't touch it, she'll never do it that well again!" How right Edens was, although Ms. Garland would sing the song many times again memorably, this is the definitive version; her joyous, euphoric exuberance would never quite be matched again.

Finally, there is the song that almost got away. The initial lyrics by Hugh Martin to "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" were rather bleak. Judy Garland who was to sing this in the film to cheer up her little sister played by Margaret O'Brien was justifiably appalled. She said if she sang that song as written to little Margaret O'Brien, the audience would think she was a monster! Garland loved the melody and asked Martin to please rewrite the words, stubbornly he refused, and she rightly wouldn't sing it as written. Thankfully, another cast member Tom Drake who played "the boy next door" talked some sense into Martin, and he changed the lyrics to be more hopefully optimistic. Don't we all owe a debt of gratitude to Ms. Garland and Mr. Drake? What a loss it would have been of one of the all-time Christmas classics, which has been recorded many times and used in many more films! Still, it's Ms. Garland's soulful, poignant rendition that will always remain the version to surpass.

Hopefully, if you're interested in the CD, you've viewed the original film at least once. If so, this soundtrack recording will double your pleasure. All of the other songs not written by the Martin/Blane team are included, exactly as performed in the film. There are both renditions of the title song, the jaunty dance number "Skip to My Lou", the charming Garland/O'Brien duet "Under the Bamboo Tree", the romantic "Over the Bannister Leaning" , and last but not least the touching duet by Mr. and Mrs. Smith "You and I". This was not only written by the film's producer Arthur Freed, but he also dubbed Leon Ames singing voice as Mr. Smith! A delightful bonus is a ballad "Boys and Girls Like You and Me" that is gorgeous, simply and enchantingly sung by Judy Garland. This song was written by Rodgers and Hammerstein for their smash Broadway hit "Oklahoma!", but it was cut out of town. Arthur Freed bought it to be used in "Meet Me in St. Louis", where Esther sings it to John Truitt as they tour the site where the World's Fair is being built. Regrettably, the powers that be felt that it slowed down the film, and also the movie needed trimming for time, so this lovely song was sacrificed. Sadly, the footage was lost, but at least we have Garland's peerless rendition as consolation.

The orchestrations by MGM's acclaimed Conrad Salinger used to underscore the film are incomparable and add immeasurably to the richness of the final film. Listening just to the background music, vivid, shining images from the film spring to the mind's eye, and you can almost hear dialogue even though none is recorded on the soundtrack. Some examples would be Esther and John lowering the lamp lights after Lon's going away party, Tootie's bizarre Halloween adventures; Grandpa's comforting the weeping Esther after John is unable to take her to the Christmas dance, and the final triumphant conclusion as the Smith family gathers at the World's Fair. My personal favorites are the music used for the Christmas sequences, the delicate, innocent proposal scene between Esther and John, Esther's and Tootie's bittersweet conversation over a tender rendition of "The First Noel" in the background that skillfully blends into the introduction to "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas." Just to give you an instance of how powerful and expertly composed are Salinger's orchestrations, is just after Esther finishes singing "Have Yourself...". Tootie rushes out to destroy the snow people, the beautiful melody of the song becomes louder, frenzied and dissonant as Tootie's hysteria builds while she knocks the snow people apart. As Esther rushes out to embrace and comfort her, the music calms into a quieter, more soothing accompaniment with an undercurrent of melancholy as Esther tries to reassure both of them that the move to New York will be a good thing even though she doesn't believe it. The final plaintive measures tug at your heartstrings as both sisters break down in each other's arms. I want to give a tip of the hat to the MGM orchestra under conductor George Stroll who perfectly realized the films' score. The restoration is outstanding, and the Stereophonic Sound is crystal clear in its clarity.

A last inducement is the four page booklet which has both publicity photos and stills from the film that accompany a nicely written background essay. If like me you're a fan of "Meet Me in St. Louis" and/or Judy Garland this is a soundtrack you will treasure and want to listen to over and over again. Hopefully it will be reissued sometime in the near future, so a whole new generation can enjoy.

reviews:
Busta Rhymes is one of those artist that cannot be duplicated, from his animated videos to his rapid fire flow to his charisma, just watch A Tribe Called Quest's classic Scenario video when Busta pops with the famous line Rah, rah, like a dungeon dragon, come on now how could you not be a fan of Busta? He's one of a kind and it shows on his debut The Coming. This album sounds like nothing else that was released at the time. The Coming is centered around that Apocalypse theme and like many others, Busta really thought the world was gonna end.

Busta still has fun on The Coming though, for instance, the singles "Woo Hah!! Got You All in Check" and "It's a Party" featuring Zhane' are fun party songs. On "The Coming Intro", he gets at people who he feels is misrepresenting Hip-Hop, and tells the ones who fell off too keep falling, Lord Have Mercy and Rampage appear as well. The interesting part about intro is that in the album booklet, "The 8th Wonder" and "Keep Falling" are labeled as tracks. So its basically three songs in one. Then on "Abandon Ship", Busta and Rampage exchange verses and they brought the best out of each other. And the song is produced by Busta himself.

Q-Tip assists Busta on The Ummah (credited as Q-Tip) produced "Ill Vibe", Q gives you food for thought (No we don't promote no guns, but don't turn that cheek/ In the world that we live calmness is viewed as weak) and Bus rips it too (Rhymes create life like the birds and the bees/ Make Funk-Master Flex say yo I'm feeling these Flows make you s*** in your drawers/ Change your dungarees). Also, check out the eight minute posse cut "Flipmode Squad Meets Def Squad" featuring Jamal, Redman, Keith Murray, Rampage & Lord Have Mercy. Trust me you won't be disappointed .

The Leaders of the New School have a reunion on "Keep It Movin'" produced by Jay Dee (The Ummah). Other dope joints are "Everything Remains Raw" produced by Easy Mo Bee and "Do My Thing" produced by DJ Scratch. As for the low points of the album, "Hot Fudge" is definitely one of them and I wasn't too big on "The Finish Line" either. Also, some of the songs are too lengthy with skits at the end. Overall The Coming is a very good album by Bussa Bus. I recommend to any Hip-Hop fan.

reviews:
Just a few highlights for me in regard to this release... The remastered and deluxe editions of both "Wild Life" and "Red Rose Speedway" were absolutely phenomenal, amazingly perfect (Booklets and doodles/sketches included!). ;)

The jolly "Tomorrow," from the original album, which also was a highlight on the Paul McCartney "Wingspan" compilation, was one of my favorites and sounds amazing in remastered form... Gotta love the sound of a piano on any Paul McCartney song. :)

Now, I'm sure I'm not the only one who noticed BUT, while the record labels usually indicate that the album was recorded in stereo, "Bip Bop" was actually a mono recording... I like how in the rough mix (Which I still can't tell is an alternate version or not, while it is indeed presented in a slightly lower key) is actually featured in stereo! The rough mix has that left-to-right reverb effect on the vocals the same way that the vocals were featured on some of the stereo mixes from the "Revolver" album by The Beatles; Ex: "I'm Only Sleeping"/"And Your Bird Can Sing"/"Doctor Robert."

The rough mix of "Mumbo" is missing those amazing high-pitched electric guitars but features a nice alternate stereo mix with the piano on the left channel and the guitars and organ on the right channel... The fade-in is pretty neat as well. :) I'm very glad that this release, as well as "Red Rose Speedway," didn't exclude any bonus tracks from the 1993 editions...

Highlights for me, in regard to the bonus material, includes "When The Wind Is Blowing," which takes me back to the "McCartney" album and would have fit in nicely as part of that album, I think... Such a calm and relaxing atmosphere to that track! I also enjoy the "peppy" instrumental alternate version of "Give Ireland Back To The Irish" with the jolly sounding electric guitars... You have to hear it for yourself! Such energy on that track. :)

The closer to the disc with bonus material, "African Yeah Yeah," is also enjoyable with the "sing-along" atmosphere... You can just tell that Paul and the gang were enjoying themselves while performing that number. :) It was also a treat to be presented with the home recordings of "Bip Bop" and "Hey Diddle," which was previously featured on "Wingspan," although some excerpts were missing or edited out on the "Wingspan" version. These are just a few of my favorite moments, and I'm sure that there are many others I will have forgotten to mention after submitting this review!

Oh, and the alternate cover photos of the members of Wings were well presented too. :) If you are a Paul McCartney and Wings completest, you will go "Wild" over this release... It is definitely worth the price for both the audio as well as the visuals. :)

Now, let's hope and pray for (HOPEFULLY) remasters/rereleases of both "London Town" and "Back To The Egg," two more favorite Wings albums of mine, as the next (Most likely!) reissues in the Paul McCartney archive collection. ;) Thanks for reading and God Bless! ~"KevyGuy" :)

"Kattorna" a disquieting music from the Danish movie by Carlssen (the title means Kittens), changes on this disc into real tour de force by Stanko, that reminds us of Mexican deguello from the siege of Alamo time. Komeda's exceptional illustrative talent made him the much valued composer of music to many movies and among them some by R. Polanski. "Svantetic", dedicated to Swedish poet Svante Forster, creates initially an impression of a dirge, but its main diatonic motif in d-minor ! reviews: This album should have been called Dylan Sings Sinatra, since most of these songs are strongly identified with Frank, recorded either at  Columbia in the late 40s or Capitol in the 50s.  I just read an interview of  Dylan in this month's AARP magazine, in which he discusses Sinatra's influence on him growing up. It is interesting that Dylan, McCartney, Streisand and myself are all 73 within a year, which means we all were young teenagers in the 50s when Sinatra was at his zenith as a singer--certainly the best of the genre. And that great period must have had an impression on them--as it did me. I know Paul has done an album recently at the old Capitol recording studios, where Sinatra recorded his famous concept LPs. I have never heard him talk about Sinatra, except to mention he had written a "funny" song for Sinatra at some point, which Frank never recorded. I know that Streisand was a fan of Frank--I recall her doing "Wee Small Hours" as her opening song in a night club performance a few years ago. And then the "I've Got a Crush on You" tape duet in her Brooklyn concert recently. And now Dylan, whose main forte is folk singing, has come to the fore. In the AARP article, he says Sinatra is the mountain which we all try to climb, or some such words. He also says that Frank sings TO you, not AT you--which is a perceptive enough comment.  As for this CD, I prefer Dylan the folk singer. The problem is nobody can really sound as good trying to sing Sinatra songs. That is too high a mountain to climb.

I was sooo sick and tired of metal bands that got comfortable with a style and never broke new ground. I figured the same result would happen with God Forbid...holy hell was i wrong!

IV : Constitution of Treason is one of the better american metal releases of the past 5 years. God Forbid breaks all boundaries in what one thinks of when it comes to metal these days. What they lacked on Gone Forever, songwriting, got an adrenaline shot to the throat with this album. There is no set pattern to any one song that is identical to another. These songs carry their own weight throughout the listen. The solos are placed perfectly, the breakdowns are never overdone, and most of all the anger is real. Hopefully this gives a wake up call to all the of the metal bands going through the motions and not really testing themselves. Howard Jones was capable of so much more on End of the Heartache and Brian Fair wimped out on War Within. Byron Davis, on the other hand, rips through with ferious vocals and anger filled yet thought provoking lyrics. The concept of the album is definitely appropriate given the state of our world right now. The story is even told in the booklet and quite a good one as well.

The CD is in my top ten for the year, and that is saying a lot considering 2005 has graced us with tons of great metal CDs. Right as I thought the American metal scene was boring and played out, God Forbid steps up to the plate and knocks a homerun that will have people talking all year and perhaps longer...

reviews:
FOUR & 1/2 STARS, but let me explain why:

For the purposes of this review, let's view Mr. Orbit's discography this way: his solo albums ["Orbit", Strange Cargo 1,2,&3 and "Pieces In A Modern Style"] along with Strange Cargo's "Hinterland", Torch Song's albums ["Wish Thing" "Ecstasy" & "Towards The Unknown Region"] and Bassomatic's ["Set The Controls For The Heart Of The Bass" & "Science And Melody"] together as one body of work.

It's been six years since 2000's "Pieces In A Modern Style" and while that was a good disc, it still wasn't up to the Strange Cargo, Torch Song & Bassomatic standards. And since they were electronic versions of classical compositions, they needn't be.

I jonesed until this album was released and I wasn't disappointed per se, but truthfully, with the exception of the single "Spirals" featuring Sugababes & Kenna - this album sounds more like the follow-up to Torch Song's 1995 Opus "Towards The Unknown Region" than a flat-out William Orbit project. Don't get me wrong, the ethereal arrangements, deep bass, exquisite processing along with his production restraint and prowess are all there - it just doesn't reach the heights of the last 3 Strange Cargo albums or Hinterland, and it doesn't come close to the work of Bassomatic at all.

Not that this is a bad thing - this is a GREAT album to chill by and provides very visual and colorful music when the listener closes their eyes - exactly what most ALL William Orbit projects promise. I guess I just wish he would ramp up again and play with my mind the way he did with the Strange Cargo series.

When I say this sounds like a follow-up to Torch Song's last album, that is literal since Laurie Mayer and Rico Conning composed 4 out of the 11 tunes and performed on 6. It is very low key, quiet, mysterious and broods just beneath the surface but never breaks through. Perhaps it wasn't meant to, I may be hanging my expectations on it.

If you love Mr. Orbit's work, [and I REALLY, REALLY do], you will like this album and it will be an integral part of his discography for the fan. I took off 1/2 a star because I am really ready for a more upbeat and mysterious production from him. If you've been to his website, he has twenty 60-second clips of unreleased songs, an unreleased song from Hello Waveforms "G-155", as well as another 28 or so unreleased tunes. These are wasted just sitting on his site, unreleased. Most of these are EXCELLENT but you cannot download these songs and it would make sense to release these as part of a 'unreleased and b-sides' disc. These songs approach more of what I was hoping Hello Waveforms was going to be.

But with all that said, this is a great disc - I just hope he doesn't take another 6 years to release another album and he finally gives his fans an album of the songs he's been teasing them with on his site. If you love Orbit, you'll love this disc but I'm waiting for more... Respectfully submitted William, and anytime you'd like to work with me on my music, in either production or mixing, the door is WIDE OPEN!
title: Hello Waveforms
description: Amazon.com, The first of what producer/composer William Orbit has described as his "binary" recordings for 2006 (this component arriving in February, the altogether different, Cellcloud, in May),, Hello Waveforms, is a work of subtle charms, brainy noodlings, and no landmark tracks. It yields understated pleasures to listeners itching to hear smartly conceived chillout electronica that evokes serenity minus lethargy (witness the percolating atmospherics of "Sea Green" and the richly textured headphone sojourn of "Who Owns the Octopus"). Yet while the overall experience is inherently enjoyable, some of Orbit's synth voices sound weirdly dated, as though an analog Moog (or Casio keyboard) had been revived to create some of the textures that swirl through his otherwise sophisticated sound fields. At such moments fans might envision this much-respected self-described "knob-twiddling producer chap" wearing an throwback athletic jersey as he injects Atari music into a PlayStation world, then packaging it all quite appropriately with a semi-psychedelic go-go fairy on the disc's cover. Often lovely, occasionally tepid, with nine instrumentals and two vocal tracks that more often float and meander rather than pulse and evolve, the slow-tempo, Hello Waveforms, stands as an intriguing project that has the ability to both engage and perplex fans of this sagacious studio wizard., --Terry Wood

reviews:
The Bee Gees albums are typicall known for containing 2 elements: lush ballads and funky, uptempo numbers. While the lush ballads have always been a personal favorite, the Brothers Gibb have also recorded some great dance/pop songs like: "Jive Talkin'", "Nights on Broadway", "You Should be Dancing", "Stayin' Alive", "Night Fever", "Tragedy", "Love You Inside Out", "He's a Liar", "The Woman in You", "You Win Again", "One", and "Paying the Price of Love".

This CD however lacks any of the percussive beats that have driven some of the Bee Gees best tunes. The closest the brothers get to anything resembling a beat are the hit single "Alone", the follow-up "Still Waters Run Deep", and album cuts "With my Eyes Closed" and "Smoke and Mirrors". All of the songs are sung in the whispered, hushed voices that they used on classic songs like "How Deep is Your Love" and "How Can You Mend a Broken Heart".

Besides the 2 singles, some of the other good cuts include "Miracles Happen", "Smoke and Mirrors", "I Surrender", "My Lovers Prayer", and "Closer Than Close". My only problem with this CD is that there is nothing here to get you up on your feet and dance. Sure, "Alone" is a great song to sing along to in the car, but there is nothing really fun and energetic about these tracks.

If you like the melodic, lush ballad side of the Bee Gees, then you will enjoy this CD. If you like the funky, dance side of the Bee Gees, there is not much here for you. However, I still recommend this CD for some great Bee Gees melodies.

reviews:
(Before you click you hated my review based on the title, please give my review a read - thanks.)

I'm not a vindictive man by any means, but when I was handed this to review and smelled the obviousness of it, my blood ran hot. I took a long look at this very compact import box set and wondered "how can I review this?"

If there is one thing about the six album six year long output of this incredible quartet from Long Beach, California, it's the music - it's both old and new, and with every play you always find a new gem to explore. I've been a fan of them since the late 1980's when I found original cassette copies of all of their albums. I knew that I had tapped into something wonderful and special, but I was just too young enough to remember their music when it first charted and it was played on my old AM radio of mine...

But now it's 2011, sadly Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years this month, and this is The Doors' 8th (EIGHTH!) incarnation of "greatest hits/total album packaging." I'm not gonna lie, I really had to step back before I wrote this review. Here's what I got, and I'm being as brief as possible.

The sound quality is okay, it sits compact on the shelf, and that's well and good, but I've heard better (more on that later) - and all you really get here is the same CD's packaged in paper sleeves with the feel of vinyl covers for all six albums. No new music, no outtakes, no new surprises, which to some might be wonderful. It's a straightforward collection of their original albums, that's it.

But this is all I can say about it.

So why put another collection again, I asked myself? I gave you the reason a few seconds ago - Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years ago this month. Why else would the three remaining members (or their lawyers) agree to put out the same albums? Here's where I got upset, but I stepped back and gave this a good reasoning:

Back in 2006 the remaining members put out the ultimate collection of all things Doors with "Perception," which was supposed to be the end-all-be-all definitive complete album set by The Doors, with sound quality on the 6 CDs (and 6 DVD-A's on the more expensive version of the set), surpassing the older 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2003 box sets and greatest hits albums by light years! They included some newer outtakes of songs never heard before, extended cuts of songs and more, with interviews and videos and hours of watching (and listening) with sound quality from the original masters so cleaned up, remastered and crystal clear in my opinion is unsurpassed by anyone since this release.

It was amazing, and I listened to it for hours, and it really took me back and it was wonderful. It's in my top twenty of what I'd bring if I was deserted on a desert island music albums...

But then I came back to earth and once again I asked "why this little no-frills set? Why put out a set 5 years after their Mount Everest, with okay quality sound at best?"

Then that nagging thought came back to me again - Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years ago this month in 1971.

Sadly, I had thought of yet another reason this was released...

Greed. Plain and simple. How much money can they extract from their fans? Only Aerosmith and Bon Jovi are more obvious, blatant and greedy to retread their hits and sell you four, five (or in this case eight) different versions of greatest hits/album collections. Their lawyers must have looked at the calendar and thought "hmm, we can make a buck or two with this... All hail the almighty cash..."

So that's it, and that's all I want to say about it without being any meaner. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE take a pass on this, because as a basic collection of The Doors albums it's nice, but they've done far far better in the past. Do yourself a massive favor and search out and find the "Perception" box set, and then drink a glass of wine (or whatever gets you to that higher plane) and relax with that.

This set is obvious, cold and really has nothing new worth picking it up for, as any real Doors fan could see the obviousness of it a mile away as well and say "no thanks."

I gave this back. You should too.

(Thanks for reading my review, and please leave any comments or votes you've got.)

reviews:
I've been a fan of Aerosmith for about four years now, and this is the fourth album by them that I've heard. Amazing or not, I like them all. The band is a legend already, and I believe that they'll be remembered as one of the greatest bands. The have their own unique sound, which you either like or not. I like it.
The album starts with Intro, a nice little piece of music. From thet we can smoothly move to Eat the Rich. The lyrics are fun, and this is a true Aerosmith rock song. After that comes the title song, Get A Grip. I have to warn you; someone burps loud at the very beginning of the song! Grip is another rock song, and Tyler's voice raises and raises in the "I get so excited" -part so that you'd think he'd explode any time. Fever comes after that; at first I didn't like the song, but then I got excited about it. Sounds to me a bit like Rolling Stones, and I also love Tyler's harmonica. Livin' On the Edge is probably the most famous song from this album, but it just doesn't chill me that much. Flesh is a bit like Fever, and once again we can hear the Demon Of Screaming at his best. This is a very energetic song. Walk On Down is Joe Perry saying "Hey I have a good song too, let's put it on the album!" I'm glad they listened to Joe as Walk On Down is easy-going but full of rock. Shut Up And Dance is one of my favorites, a rock song that makes you want to dance as they tell you to. And when you are tired after hard dancing, you can relax by listening to Cryin'. I like the song, but the live version on Little South Of Sanity is much better, it's a gem while this version sounds like a bad recording of a song that could have been better. The next song, Gotta Love It is my favourite. It rocks, has depth and power. It reminds me of Michael Jackson's Give In To Me (Dangerous, 1991), and if you like Give In... because of the song, not just because of Michael Jackson, you gotta love this song too (or other way round; if you like this you'll like Give In To Me). Crazy follows this song, another ballad which is pretty good. I'm just sad that they picked the ballads for singles, why not Flesh for example. But Aerosmith makes great ballads, so... you'll probably go crazy for this song. Line Up features Lenny Kravitz, but it's not the most interesting song in this album. Can't Stop Messin' became one of my favorites; at first I thought the beginning was too sudden, but now I can't get enough of it. Amazing, amazingly another famous slow ballad... good but don't listen to it too often so you won't get bored. Boogie Man comes silently from nowhere, stops by to float in your mind and after it has faded away it'll still float in your brain. Spooky.
I don't want to say anything stupid like "buy this cd" or "this is the best" or "vote for my review" but I don't actually know what to say. Boogie Man is still filling my mind.

We all know these are taken from records,not the original master tapes.Normally that would normally take it down a star, however my biggest bugaboo comes with the mastering of these records.They have put a rather large lid on the high end,so the sound is dead and there is no life in them.Luckily I can compare them to the Decca masters of which some have been released over the years,and there is little comparison.
There are only two pluses I can see here A) thankfully, they seem to have used the Decca's issued in the 50s, and not the later 60s and 70s re issues with that terrible reverb added.And B) AS mentioned above,they have complied all his Decca's together,but that's it.
It is just a shame that Universal hasn't issued these songs in their complete form after all these years.While the major labels sit and twiddle their thumbs on their golden cache of recordings,the "low level" outfits like Sepia take the bull by the horns and do what the majors won't;realizing a need,fulfilling it and taking away their profits.
In conclusion,while the sound is not the best at all,for the time being it is a must have set for any Jolie fan or anyone who likes just plain good music.This is Jolie at his best, when the recording techniques of the day seem to have caught up with him, and captured that beautiful deep and rich tenor voice of his.Btw,the liner notes are by noted music maven Chris Popa.

description: An appropriate title if there ever was one. Nova Scotia songbird Anne Murray is a crooner to the core, all style and grace with a capital G. As the title suggests, 1993's Croonin' is a collection of cover songs by soft-pop giants like Perry Como, Rosemary Clooney, Bing Crosby, and Peggy Lee. Murray swoons through versions of standards like "Fever," "Allegheny Moon," and "Cry Me a River," sticking as tight to the originals as possible. It's an exceptionally restrained recording, one where extravagance is some jazzy finger snapping and a lazy sax solo. Still, Murray's voice is remarkably strong and the arrangements, though subdued, are tasteful. --Matt Galloway

description: Product description, CD, Amazon.com, The last time Bruce Springsteen gave up E Street for Folk Street, the band of fiddles, banjos, and accordions--sans audience--was recording 2006's, We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions, in the informality of his living room. This time the Boss takes his American-music foray to Ireland for a three-night stint on the north quay of Dublin's River Liffey. The 23 songs drawn from those performances cover most of the songs from the Pete Seeger tribute, but venture drastically into Springsteen's popular back catalog ("Atlantic City," "Highway Patrolman," "Blinded By the Light") while delving further into his affinity for multiple styles of music, from folk and blues to gospel and country. "If I Should Fall Behind" plays like a tear-jerking last call in a dimly lit pub. "Open All Night" has been shaped into pure swing, complete with pedal steel and sax. And "Jesse James," with its furious banjo, spectator handclaps, and Springsteen howl, could pass for the Pogues, circa 1985. A simultaneously released DVD uses nine cameras to capture every sweat-beaded highlight, from the tin whistle of "Further Up the Road" to an arena bursting out in a "We Shall Overcome" singalong., --Scott Holter

reviews:
Okay, time to get in Doc Brown’s DeLorean and ride back to the past, set the meter on Leipzig (does Doc’s car ride in space too? I guess so, because as Einstein taught us, space is time is space is time) in anywhere between 1723 and 1750 (don’t forget your vaccinations – you don’t want this to be a one-way trip!).

And there, meet Bach. Disguise as a wealthy patron, a friend of Count Kayserling (who famously commissioned the Goldberg Variations) and commission a series of keyboard works from the great composer, on themes that you would provide. Which themes? Ah, those from the most favorite Beatles songs.

This is fantasy, of course and alas. There’s no going back into the past to meet all those great composers whom we love so much (and the plague and cholera), except in our imagination.

But John Bayless has done it for us, on Pro Arte CDD 346, recorded in june 1987. Not gone back to Bach in Doc’s DeLorean, but composed those keyboard works in the style of Bach on themes of the favorite Beatles songs, in fact combining themes of Bach and themes of the Beatles. And it’s very skillfully done, and very entertaining.

So this is not your customary “Beatlelized Bach”, it’s more your Bachified Beatles, Bachianas Beatlemania as it were, but it’s better, more genuinely Bach, than most such collections I’ve heard, like the apparently very popular and terribly kitsch “[[ASIN:B000056PQ2 Beatles Go Baroque]]” on Naxos, which sounds neither like fish nor like fowl, Bayless’ compositions sound very Bach indeed – integral with the fugue in “Good Day Sunshine / Daytripper”, the chorale in “If I Fell”, the Gigue in form of a Two-Part Invention in “Lady Madonna” (there one part Bach, one part Beatles) and Three-Part in “Here Comes the Sun”, the Chromatic Fantasy in “Good Day Tripper” and “A Hard Day’s Night”, Variations from the Goldbergs in “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer”, “With a Little Help from my Friends”, “Can’t Buy Me Love”, etc.– but on themes that you recognize as unmistakably the Beatles’. This is entertaining for both fans of Bach’s keyboard music and fans of the Beatles (the two groups may intersect) – although more, I think, for fans of Bach.

This is a sequel to another similar collection by Bayless, also on Pro Arte, CDD 211, [[ASIN:B000000C7W Bach Meets the Beatles]], which I absolutely must buy now – but don’t confuse with the 2004 release on the label Compendia, with the same title, [[ASIN:B0002739O0 Bach Meets the Beatles]] “revisited”, which seems to be a compendium, indeed, of the two Pro Arte CDs. And I’m going to buy loads of both to give to friends – probably fans of the Beatles more than fans of Bach. What can’t you do with a little help from your friends. TT 59 minutes.

reviews:
Since the spring of 2005, Arch Enemy have been promising that their newest album would be darker and heavier than their recent work. After the highly mixed opinions over the vocals of newcomer Angela Gossow on 2001's _Wages of Sin_, and the shorter, more streamlined styles of 2003's _Anthems of Rebellion_, the band more than lived up to that promise. Their latest effort, _Doomsday Machine_, ranks alongside Meshuggah's _Catch ThirtyThr33_ and Darkane's _Layers of Lies_ as being one of the best Swedish metal albums in the past year.

The aforementioned "streamlined" trimmings from _Anthems of Rebellion_ seem to have been put onto the back burner on _Doomsday Machine_. The Amott brothers are just as good as they've ever been, again claiming the title as one of the tightest heavy metal guitar duos of all time, with their leads, solos, and melodies much more of a throwback to their _Stigmata_ (1998) and _Burning Bridges_ (1999) days. The rhythm section is beefed up a lot more as well; Sharlee D'Angelo's bass adds a distinctively deep backdrop to the guitars, and Daniel Erlandsson (who had promised more variation in his drumming) uses his set to create rhythms that EXPLODE in bursts of thunder, even utilizing blast beats to intensify and complement the album's heaviness.

Aside from its more powerful sound, perhaps the most distinguishing and significant aspect of _Doomsday Machine_ are Angela Gossow's vocals. Without a shadow of a doubt, this is her best performance to date. She uses a lot more range this time around; she's always had range, if not as much as many a fan (spoiled on AE's original vocalist Johan Liiva) would have liked. But now she utilizes subtle dynamics in her voice to express emotion (even if all the "emotion" is just different forms of anger), presenting a much more demanding presence in the music.

As expected of Arch Enemy, there are ultra-fast songs which could well decapitate someone if they try to bang their heads in time, such as the lead single "Nemesis," "I Am Legend/Out for Blood," and "Machtkampf." "I Am Legend/Out for Blood" (undoubtedly titled after the epic Richard Matheson vampire novel) features simply demonic vocals, and an outstanding use of blast-beats in the bridge; this song alone shows Arch Enemy's death metal roots. "My Apocalypse" sports especially intricate drum work, and a well-timed break with brilliant guitar harmonies, slowly building in tempo until the song returns to its overall heaviness. Even the two instrumental tracks on this album, "Hybrids of Steel" and intro track "Enter the Machine," serve as more than just filler. The former, clocking in at almost four minutes, is a full-length composition, with back-and-forth guitar duels, nice tempo and key changes, and excellent use of harmonies.

Even the best works of an artist have their flaws, and this album is no exception. There are a couple of instances which shows a lack of fresh ideas, and only on the part of Christopher Amott. The outro lead on "Mechanic God Creation" is a blatant rehash of Michael's final solo on "Silent Wars," from _Anthems of Rebellion_. Also, the final lead on "Machtkampf" is based off of the same melody as his own solo on the _Wages of Sin_ track "Burning Angel." Perhaps Christopher just likes to play these melodies (a lot), or perhaps the band deemed these leads as being just what the songs needed, but the similarities to their older material is uncanny. Thankfully, however, these are the only low points on the album, and hardly blemish the overall work.

With the recent upheaval of attention towards Swedish metal in the United States, there have been some musical sacrifices made by bands such as In Flames and Soilwork, who were both spoiled to varying degrees by their sudden popularity. Because of the inclusion of both of these bands (as well as Arch Enemy themselves) on the Ozzfest '05 bill, many a fan has begun to think that the future of Swedish metal was looking grim. However, through _Doomsday Machine_, Arch Enemy show no signs of slowing down, softening up, or any other qualities which could be used to label the band as "selling out." Having finally found the proper formulas which work best for their music, Arch Enemy have released their best album since _Burning Bridges_. It only can get better from here.

title: The Traveling Wilburys Collection
description: Product Description, Featuring classics like "Handle With Care," "End Of The Line," and "Heading For The Light," super-group Traveling Wilbury's Collection highlights all of the band's music and previously unreleased bonus tracks through this re-mastered double album. The DVD features behind the scenes footage of the band writing and recording, along with their 5 video clips., Amazon.com, The Traveling Wilburys were one of the few supergroups that lived up to their promise, because they didn't try to. Things started inauspiciously when George Harrison, needing a B-side for a 1988 single, called in friends Jeff Lynne, Bob Dylan, Tom Petty, and Roy Orbison for assistance. Two albums later--the second without Orbison, who had passed away shortly after the first was released--the loose-knit collective had recorded material that was as durable, and occasionally eclipsed, the participants' legendary solo work. The Wilburys succeeded due to a genial and contagious camaraderie that permeates both discs. What could have been a train wreck of ego clashes instead resulted in a frothy meeting of the minds. These guys are having a blast, trading lead vocals and harmonies on energetic folk-rock, quirky rockabilly, and Beatlesque pop that shimmers with the respect and esteem the members clearly hold for each other. Harrison and Lynne's rather slick production polishes off edges that might better have been left unvarnished, but there's no denying the loosey-goosey craftsmanship at work in tunes such as "Handle with Care," "End of the Line," and a striking Orbison performance on "Not Alone Anymore" that ranks with any of his finest. Both albums were million-sellers, but oddly went out of print for about a decade until Rhino resurrected them, adding two rare tracks per disc as well as a DVD of music videos and a band documentary. The resulting package is a comprehensive overview of a once--well, twice--in-a-lifetime project that, especially after Harrison's passing, will never be repeated., --Hal Horowitz

reviews:
Early Funkadelic released some seriously brilliant and completely wigged-out albums, and this very well may be the craziest of them all. It's also the second-best of the mighty early Westbound triumvirate (Funkadelic, Free Your Mind, the astounding Maggot Brain). The later Westbound comp "Music For Your Mother" is also fantastic, featuring a lot of the songs on these albums in far superior mixes.

The CD remastering - for the American version of the CD - is awful, which is practically a crime and saps much of the power out of a glorious acid-funk masterpiece. Unforgivable? Yes. But this doesn't hold true for all issues of the album. My advice is simple. Get The British Version Of This Album. It sounds amazing. Granted, the production and mixing themselves still get in the way, because, like the music, they too were done on acid, but at least with the British version it doesn't sound flatter than a waffle. Instead, it sounds full-bodied and even warm on some of the songs.

The first track, "Free Your Mind And Your Ass Will Follow," is tripped out into regions beyond. Certainly, these were intergalactic Funkateers not of this planet. Are those synth noises at the beginning, or are they just processed feedback? I don't know, but whatever it is, it's brilliant. Then the groove comes in - Tiki Fulwood, possibly the best drummer Funkadelic ever had, comes in with an implacable and totally funky drum entrance, spurring them all into the acid-freakout-funk jam. The screams and LSD-fueled chants are drugged Detroit soul of the purest form, and Eddie Hazel's searing, unutterably awesome and wholly, terrifyingly Hendrix-like guitar work rips out of the speakers, competing with Bernie Worrell's fuzzed-out quasi-classical Hammond organ for dominance. This continues for the rest of the 10 minutes. "Friday Night, August 14th" follows with a bluesy acid-funk shuffle, with more brilliant and radical guitarin' from the Eddie Hazel-Tawl Ross guitar tag team. Fulwood's semi-drum-solo, fed through abusive amounts of analog echo and delay, caps a great song. "Funky Dollar Bill" would be great, but there is a problem. It's all fantastic - the rhythm guitar is unbelievable, the lead bluesy and paint-strippingly loud - but the Worrell jangle-piano part is terrible, I'm sorry to say. It's a painfully obvious overdub, and it's badly out-of-tune and nearly out-of-rhythm; it ruins the song for me, sadly. All is forgiven with THE JAM OF ALL TIME, "I Wanna Know If It's Good To You." The vocal part is amazing, but the instrumental jam afterwards is what really rips me to shreds. That guitar soloing is simply on a plane beyond what most soloists could even think of reaching - the best feedback entrance ever. Ever. Signed, sealed, and delivered. It's also sweet as hell when it all quiets down, Fulwood starts hitting the cowbells in totally funky rhythm (More Cowbell!!!), suddenly the mix turns better, and Billy "Bass" Nelson's astoundingly funky bass playing becomes audible - those trills alone could make you dance like a funky fool. "Some More" comes after that, and predictably can't really compare, as it's a jokey blues song, but it's fun enough - the vocal effects are great, and it's better than "Back In Our Minds" on "Maggot Brain." "Eulogy and Light" is really freaky, and ends the album with a slowed-down and massively reverbed Clinton monologue from the view of a pimp (I guess; I'm not sure, really) showing worship to the God "Big Buck" over a really scary backwards tape; the music is from an old 1969 B-side, "Open Our Eyes," which is God-praising gospel so uncut, so heartfelt, so, well, soulful that it seems like a near-perversion of religion to use it backwards for this terrifying rant, which ends with the tape being sped up as Clinton screams "Is Truth the Light?!?!?!??!!!," showing the pimp's figurative, Divine punishment. A brilliant move on Clinton's part, "Eulogy and Light" ends the album.

Such a brilliant album, even though it's painfully short at 31 minutes, deserves to be heard by everybody. Get the British version, turn "I Wanna Know If It's Good To You" up and feel the light sear your senses. I love Funkadelic.

description: Fire Make Thunder marks the fourth undertaking for the collaborative duo known as OSI. Formed in 2002 by Jim Matheos and Kevin Moore, OSI is a long distance partnership, both musicians typically writing and recording alone and sending song ideas back and forth for further elaboration. Written and recorded throughout most of 2011, this latest release once again reflects the eclectic influences of both Matheos and Moore. Returning as the bands session drummer is Gavin Harrison of Porcupine Tree, this time co-writing one of the tracks with the band. All other instruments and programming were performed by both Matheos and Moore, while vocals and lyrics were handled exclusively by Moore. All of the recording for Fire Make Thunder, with the exception of drums, was done by Moore and Matheos at each musician s respective home studio with drums being recorded at Harrison s home in London. Final overdubs as well as some additional writing/arranging was completed in July 2011 in Jamaica, Iowa where the band mixed alongside engineer matt Sepanic at Sound Farm Studio and recording Environment. Mastering was handled by renowned engineer Roger Siebel. The record was produced by both Moore and Matheos.

This is a great addition to the Opera fan's library.
It has only selections from Wagner's Magnum Opus, "The Ring of the Niebelungs". But the selections are those that most fans of Wagner's opera will recognize. What opera fan would fail to remember "The Ride of the Valkyries"? But these selections have no words, maiking hearing the music behind the lyrics even easier for the Opera fan.
And what Opera fan hasn't tried to sing in the shower? The only "fault" (if there is one) to this album is that there are no lyrics in the liner notes to complement the music - which would have made this the world's first opera karaoke.
Fans of Wagner will really get to listen to the music, which can occasionally be almost drowned out by famous singers who can overpower the orchestra. And it provides a good introduction to Wagner's "Ring" cycle - a compilation of almost 15 CD's if one were to buy the entire opera cycle, since each of the parts is almost an opera in itself.
Well worth adding to an opera fan's library, or to classical music radio stations who would not otherwise provide "opera" to their listeners.

The idea of covering folk/country/bluegrass standards and classic rock-era songs, using vintage string instruments and a free-form approach, is an excellent one. Regrettably, Messrs. Grisman, Hartford and Seeger don't quite pull it off. As you'd expect, the musicianship is beyond reproach, but the guys are guilty of straining their artistic license to the max.
The trio fares best with reverent versions of "Uncle Pen," "Windy Mountain" and "Blue Ridge Cabin Home," among others. It's when they put their tongues in their cheeks that the trouble begins. I love John Hartford, but I'm sorry, his eccentric phrasing and vocalizing on "Memphis" and "Maybelline" is hard to take. Chuck Berry is rolling over, and he ain't even dead. And what Hartford does to the sacrosanct bluegrass anthem "Rocky Top" is nothing short of criminal.
There are some outstanding tracks, notably Mike Seeger's stark vocal/banjo arrangement of Dylan's "Maggie's Farm," which Seeger sings like an angry, desperate man with no hope left. He is utterly convincing, also, on the Ralph Stanley mainstay "Room at the Top of the Stairs."

reviews:
Listeners of this particular Styx Cd must realize and understand that this is a mix of cover music material. Alot of the old time Rockers are coming out with these types of albums. It may indeed be an easy way to fullfill a record contract or more importantly a way of expressing their musical versatality. The muscianship is where this album shines the most !!!!

All you need to do is listen to this with an appreciative ear. The choice of material and the performances are expertly done. Big Bang Theory is a well produced and thought out album. Sit back, crank up the volume and appreciate the Great versions of these Rock n Roll classics being performed by well versed musicians.

The best tunes in this compilation:

1. " I Am The Walrus " Fantastic version of a Beatle classic. Close your eyes and hear John Lennons voice. That is how good Tommy Shaw is as a vocalist. All the guys stay true to the original. The arrangement and tempo are near perfect. Best of all is the fact that this is a Live version. Which sounds GREAT !!!!

2. " I Can See For Miles " A lively version of a classic Who song. Vocals, bass and drums are the stand outs. Again they stay true to the Who's original.

3. " Cant Find My Way Home " What a Cool song to choose for the album. A Fine rendition of Blind Faiths. Creative drumming and solid guitar work keep it true !!!!

4. " I Dont Need No Doctor " Is this really Styx ? These guys are so good at pulling off other peoples music. This is a hard Rocker. A classic Rock song for sure. Humble Pie also recorded a Great Live version of this.

5. " One Way Out " WOW ---- Styx the southern rock band. YES, " You Heard Right "

This literally sounds like an Allman Brothers tribute band. The drumming !!!! The dual guitar leads !!!! WOW !!!!

6. " Summer In The City " A 60's pop song with all the soul of the original. A soulful classic performed by Styx {the cover band}.

7. " Mannic Depression " Any band should be very careful when choosing to duplicate the likes of Jimi Hendrix. Drumming and Bass guitar parts are in fine form. BUT, Styx fails to match Jimi's master guitar and soulful vocals unfortunately. However, we must give them credit for trying.

8. " Locomotive Breath " Jethro Tull at it's Best. A solid version except for the lack of Ian Andersons flute solo. Styx should have enlisted the help of a guest flute player to really take this to the top. Otherwise it offers Superb musicianship AGAIN !!!!

9. " Blue Collar Man " The least favorite in my opinion. It lacks the drive and intensity of the original Styx version from the album Pieces Of Eight. It does offer a more acoustic version. Tommy Shaw does a Great job vocally. Keyboards and guitars are worthwhile also. You must listen to this a couple times for this particular version to grow on you.

Finally: " Big Bang theory " is Styx the cover band. Whoever chooses to buy this Cd MUST realize this very important fact. Styx is duplicating the music of other Great artist and that is no easy task. To the piont---- most of these songs DO NOT sound like Styx and that is what makes this Cd so Good. When any musician decides to play someone elses music. They better do a good job and Styx does a " GREAT JOB " at staying as faithful as possible to the originals.

A Masterful work of musicianship !!!!

Weezer can be too stubborn for their own good. An odds and sods release from them has potential since the size of Cuomo's unreleased material easily outweighs what is already out there, but they continue to dish out their most pedestrian tracks. With each spin, some of these songs rise above the "Dead Letter Office" quality, but there is still a whole lot of interesting stuff out there that we are not hearing.

Lyrically, I lost count of how many times I cringed ("Losing My Mind," "Blowing My Stack"). Musically, the sound can range from annoyingly saccharine ("The Odd Couple," "Autopilot," "I'm a Robot") to average/not bad (most everything else). Overall, it sounds like this "album" lacks a significant amount of forethought, which is strange considering how long the gestation period was (working title was the far less embarrassing "Odds & Ends").

The thing is, I liked the Green/"Maladroit" era. Yeah, I know it wasn't outstanding, but Weezer had momentum then and I wanted to hear more from that productive period. But most of "Death to False Metal" feels too thin to be anything more than a major label kiss-off.

reviews:
I didn't really like "The Fame", Lady Gaga's first album. I'm not a huge fan of mindless electro-trance. A few of the songs were ok, especially "The Fame" (song), but other than that it was unmemorable. And in my opinion, Lady Gaga was unmemorable throughout the time the album was mostly successful. But then something happened and she changed from "crazed slut" to "hmmm, odd" and then suddenly to "one word: unstoppable".
Even 3 months ago I wasn't impressed by her, but right now she is my favourite artist in the world.
The Fame Monster is an extremely extravagant album, and is a 5 star one at that. Here's why:
1. The lyrics are out there, and also hold real meaning, and each song has a different story to share. Each track is like a great big novel wrapped into several minutes of music.
2. The artist hasn't forgotten the fundamentals of music - the music itself. Each song is rich, rich, rich with beautiful and catchy melodies. And each track has a different style to its music. You've heard nothing like this before.
3. Each track goes for over 4 minutes and despite the fact that there are only 8 tracks, it doesn't even matter.

Lady Gaga is now about delivering gold. She really cares about her music. She is a true artist, and it's refreshing that in this day and age of boring nobody's trying to shove themselves into the limelight, somebody can come along and steal their thunder. Somebody who DESERVES it.
They're saying Gaga is the new Madonna. Well I was never a fan of Madonna, but I definitely think she is the next big thing. She's one of those people who will be remembered for decades to come. Not because she was out there. But because her music was great. Is great.

She is a keeper and this album is insanely good. I literally love every track. Everybody I know who loves this album has "a Monster song". That is, one of the 8 tracks is their personal favourite. It's almost like if somebody names their favourite song from this album, I try and analyse their decision and what kind of a person it makes. Like good psychology. My favourite is Speechless by the way, which has got to be one of the most original songs written in a long time... possibly since My Heart Will Go On, or Don't Speak. It's amazing. Here's a list of my favourites in order:

1. Speechless (gold - this is really a heartfelt song, Gaga wrote it in desperation to her father as a plea to get life-saving surgery. Instead of a sappy ballad she's gone for a rock ballad and there are just no words. This song isn't favoured by critics, but they are foolish because it's instantly catchy. A future classic, popular or not. So many layers to the song - something I always love in songs. The half-way point marks a dramatic power infusion in an already powerful song, and it carries it all the way to the end. I can't rave enough about it.)
2. Bad Romance (big, long song with (again) many layers - it's almost like a song they would play to Greek Gods)
3. Dance in the Dark (not just a great message in the song about intimacy, but also a stellar tune - it could pass as a classic '80s tune, and if it becomes a single, who knows? Maybe it will be a future classic)
4. Alejandro (reminds me of "I Come From A Land Down-Under" with the opening bit, but this is a fun song, and also sports a really, really catchy melody)
5. Teeth (mad song, mad and unforgiving - there are times Gaga sounds like Aguilera, and this song sounds similar to the opening song in "Holes"; very powerful nonetheless)
6. Monster (a really powerful song, I honestly have no idea what it's about unless she is dating Frankenstein, but it is a full-blown electro-ballad with a hint of spice in the lyrics, and it just simply rocks)
7. So Happy I Could Die (I feel bad that this is second-last on the list, because it is such a great song, but this just shows how good the album is. Powerful and catchy)
8. Telephone (all about wanting to just let go and have fun instead of dealing with a pestering significant other - great chorus and would be good in clubs. Unlike Beyonce's brother-song, this actually has substance)

Hope my review was worth it. This album is just amazing. Not a single moment to dislike. I wish every song could be a single. I would love to see what she brings to it with her surreal video clips.

reviews:
Dear Agony came out around the time that Three Day's Grace's latest, Life Starts Now, was released. I bought TDG's CD first because I'm a big fan of that band, but was disappointed in the album. I then bought Dear Agony. If there is some sort of emo competition between those two bands, Breaking Benjamin won this round! "Lights Out," alone, is awesome! One of the best songs I've heard in a while. The brutality of the lyrics, the power of the music; it's great! The CD is also pretty solid, for the most part. It has a fresh, accessible sound that does not lose its edge--well, except maybe during the title track which, surprisingly, is the weakest song on the album. I hope it won't be getting a ton of radio play. Currently "I Will Not Bow," a much better song, has been dominating the airwaves. BB reminds me of Ill Nino with the screaming vocals within the catchy tracks. The packaging is also superior to Life Starts Now. There are glossy, color photos of all the band members. Benjamin Burnley and Aaron Fink are good-looking guys. There is a photo of Burnley's late grandfather to whom the album is dedicated. He is wearing a uniform and there is at least an indirect soldier theme with some of these songs with lyrics like "carry the wounded and shut your eyes" (Into The Nothing), "leave the lost and dead behind" (I Will Not Bow), and "Live! Fight! Crawl back inside" (Crawl).

1. "Fade Away"--Killer opening with a futuristic sound.
2. "I Will Not Bow"--I've been hearing this on the radio a lot lately. It has a blistering heavy opening but then tones down to become more accessible.
3. "Crawl"--Ill Nino-esque with blood-curdling screams in between catchy heavy rock riffs. Actually, I could hear Ill Nino doing this track.
4. "Give Me A Sign"--Slower rocker with a dark romantic side, I guess, ("I'll keep you alive if you show me the way"). It is rather repetitive. There's a line in the chorus where it sounds like it's going to end only to start up again. It is not one of my favorites.
5. "Hopeless"--Another blistering, screaming hard rocker like "Crawl."
6. "What Lies Beneath"--The lyrics belie the pleasant melody: "Your sick, twisted smile...your cold, jaded eyes...you're the devil in disguise." I like that. Still, even with all those faults, "I will always be here for the rest of my life."

7. "Anthem of the Angels"--As the title suggests, there is some pretty orchestration in this track. It doesn't lose its edge, though. I like the chorus and the guitar during the bridge.
8. "Lights Out"--Awesome! Powerful, angry lyrics and a brutal, yet catchy, melody. This song is definitely the highlight of the CD. Check out these lyrics: "After the lights go out on you / After your worthless life is through / I will remember how your scream." Wow!
9. "Dear Agony"--As incredibly powerful as the last track was, it is followed by a remarkably lame-sounding track. It is the title track so, since the band thought enough of it to name the whole CD after it, it should be the highlight, right? Well, IMO, it is actually the weakest song on the album. It reminds me of "Lost In You," the lamest song on Three Days Grace's latest CD.
10. "Into The Nothing"--Now, back to the program: a good, straight-forward, power rocker.
11. "Without You"--Nice ending. The usual dark, desperate emo lyrics but I really like the line "Sing something new / I have nothing left." Orchestra closes it out.

reviews:
I've been hearing this album since it came out in 1959. My late father, who spent the better part of two decades as an off-and-on professional jazz musician, considered this album, along with its companion album "Back to Back," one of the mainstays of his jazz collection.

There isn't a whole lot I can add to what has been already said. Every artist on this album is stellar, but a few bear additional mention: Ellington showcases one of his best performances as a pianist here. While some might fault his technical skill (though I can't see why), no pianist before or since had the same way of attacking a chord as Duke. He was also great at swinging, and could "comp" other soloists just about as well as anyone.

Johnny Hodges--what you can one say? Probably in the top 5 jazz saxophonists of all time, he shines here. He had a beautiful tone, but could swing with the best. Here he is most delightful doing what he did best--delivering swinging solos on a couple of nice ballads. As an example, "Just a Memory" showcases Hodges, along with his tenor-playing lion of a counterpart, Ben Webster.

Two great trumpeters grace this album--Roy Eldridge, the underrated trumpeter best known for his vocal and trumpet duet with Anita O'Day on "Let Me Off Uptown"; and Harry "Sweets" Edison, whose trademark was never playing two notes when one would do--and still outswinging just about any other trumpeter of his era.

As another said, this album is a "jazz essential." Like they say, if you have to ask what jazz is, you'll never know. If this album doesn't tell you what it is, you'll never figure it out. This album says it all.
title: Side By Side
description: Product Description, Johnny returned to Duke-and Duke returned to a small-group format-on these marvelous 1958 and 1959 sessions, featuring premier players like Harry "Sweets" Edison, Jo Jones, Roy Eldridge, Ben Webster and Billy Strayhorn., Amazon.com, The sound of Johnny Hodges's alto saxophone--a tone of ethereal smoothness combined with slyly familiar blues phrasing and a capacity for both wit and romance--may be the most identifiable sonic marker of Duke Ellington's music, and it's much in evidence on the two small group sessions on this CD. One, from 1959, has Hodges and Ellington in a sextet with two great Basie alumni, drummer Jo Jones and trumpeter, Harry "Sweets" Edison, . The combination generates extraordinary swing, especially on the opening "Stompy Jones," with Ellington's percussive chords and Jones's drums generating enough power to drive a big band. Hodges and Edison maintain the big-band illusion, fuelling one another's solos with supportive riffs, while Ellington seems to revel in the wide-open spaces, soloing on "Going Up" with an expansive and almost casual brilliance. Though Duke is absent from the second date on this CD, featuring a septet recorded in 1958, his alter ego, Billy Strayhorn, plays piano in appropriately ducal fashion. This band has an even stronger Ellington flavor, with tenor saxophonist, Ben Webster, and trombonist Lawrence Brown adding their unique sounds to a joy-filled session that recalls Duke's small group recordings of the '30s., --Stuart Broomer

reviews:
Boggia's recent Myspace/podcast covers-- including Queen, the Faces, his glorious instructional podcast for the backing vocals to the Kinks' Waterloo Sunset-- provide a glimpse of the guy's encyclopedic visceral understanding of all that is good and tuneful and warm and human about rock'n'roll. He oozes this stuff out onto this platter, generous heaping helpings and y'all come back for seconds. He describes the record as having two sides (like vinyl), with one side about things that happened to him, one about things that happened to other people. But to me, the whole record is (sort of like all his work) a love song to his (and my) record collection. In "Listening to NRBQ," a song that will take you back to 1974 and driving around in your Camaro listening to music with your girlfriend even if you weren't born yet, he gets to a line that goes, "Then Big Al took a solo and it went like this." And if you've been paying attention to Boggia's career, then you don't even have to look at the credits because you know, you just KNOW, that yes, that's Big Al from NRBQ taking that solo.

Brilliant melodies (I'm talking, Paul McCartney brilliant), great vocal arrangements, winning songs, tasteful playing. Run, son't walk, to your nearest online retailer and grab a copy.
title: Misadventures in Stereo
description: Misadventures In Stereo, the third album by widely lauded singer/songwriter/multi-instrumentalist Jim Boggia, is unmistakably the work of a true believer and pop craftsman who's closely acquainted with music's capacity for transcendent uplift. His songs get the balance right between devastating beauty and sadness, and the big fat joke that is life. Born blind in one eye and with limited vision in the other, Boggia grew up an only child with an acutely developed ear for music. His early fascination for such iconoclastic pop classics as the Kinks' Village Green Preservation Society, Nilsson Sings Newman and Stevie Wonder's Innervisons helped to inform an aesthetic sensibility that would push him to create album-length listening experiences on his own releases. Boggia has gained impressive career momentum in a short amount of time. Blackberry selected one of his tracks for a new ad campaign and his songs have also been featured on MTV's Real World and ABC-TV's Men In Trees. He's developed a loyal grass-roots fan base for his dynamic, improvisational live shows. His work has been embraced by numerous fellow artists and kindred spirits, many of who have lent their talents to Boggia's albums. His sophomore release, Safe In Sound (2005, bluhammock music), featured key contributions from such notable admirers as Aimee Mann, Jill Sobule, MC5 guitar hero Wayne Kramer, Attractions drummer Pete Thomas and legendary '70s cult-pop icon Emitt Rhodes. Boggia's first two releases, 2002's Fidelity Is the Enemy and 2005's Safe In Sound, established him as a critical favorite. Harp magazine described his songs as "captivating," adding that he "delivers the sort of intelligent, melodic pop music that ought to be a staple of radio playlists." Paste called Boggia a "first-rate audio architect" and praised his use of "lush instrumental flourishes, intriguing sound bites and naturalistic found sounds." The Washington Post made note of his "soulful voice, experimental instrumentation and an encyclopedic knowledge of pop music." The qualities that have endeared Boggia to fans, critics and his fellow musicians are abundant throughout Misadventures In Stereo (which, appropriately, was mastered at London's fabled Abbey Road studios where the Beatles recorded virtually all of their '60s classics). His knack for merging melodic bliss and bittersweet, richly detailed lyrical substance is prominent on such tracks as the ironically jaunty-sounding "Johnnie's Going Down," the pensive "No Way Out" and the dreamily melancholy "So." Another standout is the baroque-pop underdog anthem "Chalk One Up for Albert's Side," which Boggia co-wrote with Tony Asher, legendary lyricist of the Beach Boys' landmark Pet Sounds. Particularly affecting is the haunting album-closer "Three Weeks Shy," about a soldier killed three weeks before completing his tour of duty. Boggia s deep and abiding affection for classic pop is apparent on "Listening to NRBQ," a poignant reminiscence of a love affair strengthened by a mutual love for music. The song also doubles as a tribute to the title band, whose beloved guitarist Big Al Anderson plays guitar on the track. "8Track" and "It's Your Birthday" (the latter co-written with David Poe) further examine the role that music plays in our lives and loves. With Misadventures, Boggia shows a career artist at the peak of his creative power, a self-proclaimed music geek for whom making music is as effortless as breathing. In a perfect world, everyone will be hearing more about Jim Boggia.

title: Seven Secrets
description: Product Description, The last recording of legendary jazz fusion pioneer Larry Coryell is the all new 11th House album "Seven Secrets" which will be released on June 2nd. Guitarist Coryell assembled founding 11th House members Randy Brecker (trumpet), long-timer John Lee (bass), the addition of son Julian (guitar) and the late Alphonse Mouzon (drums) to bring the rock and funk back to jazz again with a batch of eleven powerhouse tracks., Review, In January, he went into a studio in St. Augustine, Florida, and recorded a new Eleventh House project titled Seven Secrets (Savoy/429 Records) with charter members from 1973: Randy Brecker on trumpet and Alphonse Mouzon (1948 2016) on drums, along with John Lee (bassist on the group s 1975 album Level One and 1976 follow-up, Aspects) and Coryell s son Julian, a six-string shredder in his own right, on second guitar.The results, which will be released in June, are electrifying. Fueled by Mouzon s big-as-a-house back-beats and power-precision fills, Daddy Coryell cuts loose with sheer abandon on several cuts, like his Mr. Miyake and Mouzon s kinetic 7/4 title track. Coryell deals in audacious string-bending on the blues-rocker The Dip and the earthy Mudhen Blues, and delivers some Wes Montgomery-style octaves on the mellow Having Second Thoughts. But the real killer on Seven Secrets is Lee s Dragon s Way, a 6/8 romp that will whet the appetites of true fusion fans. Sparked by Mouzon s slamming groove and Lee s slippery, singing tones on his resounding Rob Allen fretless bass (with ebony fingerboard and nylon strings), this catchy number also showcases the young Julian s mondo chops, which are coming directly out of the Steve Vai Joe Satriani school. Papa Coryell follows those mind-blowing fusillades with something simple, lyrical, tasty and blue a typically Zen response from the guitar master. --Downbeat

reviews: The *raison d'etre* for this reissue can be put into two words: Carlo Bergonzi. He never recorded Nemorino, one of his finest roles, on commercial LP, so Sony's excavation from the Metropolitan Opera broadcast vaults fills a major void in the catalogue. Always a charming, vulnerable and richly Italianate interpreter of Nemorino, Bergonzi is in peak vocal form here, primed to give his recorded competition a run for their money. Nobody else here is quite on this empyrean level, although Fernando Corena's expert *buffo* stylings as Dr. Dulcamara are really only marred by spread tone in the upper register. Roberta Peters is a soubrettish Adina, less sympathetic than some, but she is an underrecorded artist, so that also makes this a valuable document. The Met's utility baritone, Frank Guarrera, sings Sgt. Belcore with rawhide tone and a personality to match (how unfortunate that Mario Sereni was unavailable) but he is competent and certainly does not sink the ship. Thomas Schippers keeps things moving lightly, displaying his usual flair for the bel canto repertory. No liner notes, just a track listing and photos of the artists.

title: SERPENT ONLY LIES
description: 2016 release, the 11th album from the metal band. For nearly three decades, the name Crowbar has been synonymous with heavy. Since rising ominously from the swamplands of New Orleans in 1990, they've been hailed internationally as one of the world's foremost purveyors of crushing, melodic sludge. The Serpent Only Lies is both an affirmation of the band's staying power and a nod to their legacy. "To me, it's a fresh-sounding version of old school Crowbar," says vocalist, guitarist and mastermind Kirk Windstein. "I intentionally went back and listened to a lot of old Crowbar stuff, like the self-titled and Broken Glass albums, to get a feel for what my mindset was 20-plus years ago. I also went back and listened to the bands that influenced Crowbar in the beginning, like Trouble, Saint Vitus, Melvins, and the first Type O Negative record. So it was kinda me doing my homework." The result is an album that stands toe to toe with those early Crowbar classics while maintaining the lumbering hooks of mid period standouts like 1998's Odd Fellows Rest and 2000's Equilibrium. Bolstered by massive riffage, new songs "I Am The Storm," "Embrace The Light" and the title track explore the themes of life, loss and spirituality, respectively. "Even lyrically, the approach was a little more old school," Windstein offers. "Some of the songs have less lyrics to let the riffs breathe a little more, which I had kind of gotten away from over the years. It was a conscious thing to go back to that."
